## Proof

Let the box have edge lengths $3, 4, 6$. It rests on one face; call the base dimensions $p\times q$ and the height $h$, where $\{p,q,h\}=\{3,4,6\}$. Place the floor as the $xy$-plane with the base occupying $[0,p]\times[0,q]$ and the box extending up to height $h$.

The light direction $\mathbf d$ is a unit vector making $45^\circ$ with the floor, so its vertical component is $|\mathbf d\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}|=\sin 45^\circ=1/\sqrt2$ and its horizontal component has magnitude $1/\sqrt2$.

**Shadow geometry.** Under parallel projection along $\mathbf d$ onto the floor, a point $(x,y,z)$ maps to $(x,y)-z\,\mathbf d_{\text{horiz}}/d_z$. The top face (at height $h$) is therefore the base rectangle translated by a horizontal vector $\mathbf v$ of length
$$|\mathbf v|=h\cdot\frac{|\mathbf d_{\text{horiz}}|}{|d_z|}=h\cdot\frac{1/\sqrt2}{1/\sqrt2}=h.$$
The full shadow is the convex hull of the base rectangle $R=[0,p]\times[0,q]$ and its translate $R+\mathbf v$.

Writing $\mathbf v=(v_x,v_y)$ in the base's axis directions (take $v_x,v_y\ge 0$ by symmetry), the convex hull is a hexagon with vertices
$$(0,0),\ (p,0),\ (p{+}v_x,v_y),\ (p{+}v_x,q{+}v_y),\ (v_x,q{+}v_y),\ (0,q).$$
A shoelace computation gives its area as
$$\text{Area}(\text{hull})=pq+p\,v_y+q\,v_x.$$
The base of the box (area $pq$) lies on the floor and must be excluded, so
$$\text{Shadow}=p\,v_y+q\,v_x.$$

**Optimizing the direction.** Since $|\mathbf v|=h$, write $v_x=h\cos\alpha$, $v_y=h\sin\alpha$. Then
$$\text{Shadow}=p\,h\,|\sin\alpha|+q\,h\,|\cos\alpha|=A_a|\sin\alpha|+A_b|\cos\alpha|,$$
where $A_a=ph$ and $A_b=qh$ are the areas of the two side faces. The maximum over $\alpha$ is
$$\max_\alpha \text{Shadow}=\sqrt{A_a^2+A_b^2}.$$

**Choosing which face is the base.** We evaluate the three choices:

| Base | $h$ | Side faces | $\sqrt{A_a^2+A_b^2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $4\times6$ | $3$ | $12,\,18$ | $\sqrt{468}=6\sqrt{13}\approx21.6$ |
| $3\times6$ | $4$ | $12,\,24$ | $\sqrt{720}=12\sqrt5\approx26.8$ |
| $3\times4$ | $6$ | $18,\,24$ | $\sqrt{900}=30$ |

The maximum is attained with the $3\times4$ face on the floor (height $6$) and the horizontal light direction satisfying $\tan\alpha=24/18=4/3$, i.e. $\cos\alpha=3/5$, $\sin\alpha=4/5$:
$$\text{Shadow}=18\cdot\tfrac45+24\cdot\tfrac35=\tfrac{72+72}{5}\cdot\tfrac{...}{}$$
More directly: $18\cdot\frac45+24\cdot\frac35=\frac{72}{5}+\frac{72}{5}=\frac{144}{5}$ — wait, let me recompute: $18\cdot\frac45=\frac{72}{5}=14.4$ and $24\cdot\frac35=\frac{72}{5}=14.4$, sum $=28.8$. That is not $30$.

Let me recheck. The maximum of $A_a|\sin\alpha|+A_b|\cos\alpha|$ is $\sqrt{A_a^2+A_b^2}$, attained at $\tan\alpha=A_a/A_b$ (so that $|\sin\alpha|=A_a/\sqrt{A_a^2+A_b^2}$, $|\cos\alpha|=A_b/\sqrt{A_a^2+A_b^2}$). With $A_a=18$, $A_b=24$:
$$|\sin\alpha|=\frac{18}{30}=\frac35,\qquad |\cos\alpha|=\frac{24}{30}=\frac45.$$
$$\text{Shadow}=18\cdot\frac35+24\cdot\frac45=\frac{54}{5}+\frac{96}{5}=\frac{150}{5}=30.\ \checkmark$$

(I had swapped $\sin$ and $\cos$ in the quick check above; the correct assignment gives $30$.)

Therefore the largest possible shadow area, excluding the base, is

$$\boxed{30}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
